sections.h2: What is the first step to sell a house in Maryland Heights, MO?
sections.html:
Request a residential occupancy inspection from the city. Maryland Heights requires an inspection and an occupancy permit at every change of ownership, so every sale runs through this step.

This rule shapes how fast a Maryland Heights sale can go. A buyer who needs repairs sorted before the city will sign off, or a seller who has never read the city's property maintenance checklist, can lose weeks. The city's inspection fee is $75 and covers up to two re-inspections. Anyone with an interest can apply, and the city has no preference as to who does: the owner, a real estate agent with the owner's permission, a property manager or a person holding power of attorney. In some HUD or foreclosure sales, the buyer applies.

Because this inspection is a fixed step, a buyer who purchases as-is and handles any corrections afterward can shorten the timeline. Sellers who prefer to list should book the inspection early, ideally before the first showing.

sections.h2: How does the Maryland Heights occupancy inspection work?
sections.html:
The inspector checks the interior and exterior, usually in less than an hour, against the city's property maintenance standards. You are given a fixed appointment time when you schedule.

  • Apply with the Application for Residential Occupancy Inspection, a copy of a photo ID, and either an email to cst@marylandheights.com, a visit to the Government Center at 11911 Dorsett Road, or a mailed packet.
  • Someone must be at the house during the inspection. A lockbox is not allowed, and anyone other than the owner or applicant must be named as an authorized representative on the form.
  • If problems are found, the inspector leaves a Field Correction Notice. The items must be fixed and the house re-inspected.
  • After the house passes, the new occupant has 90 days to obtain the occupancy permit, or a new inspection may be required.

The permit itself is separate. The buyer or tenant applies with the permit application, proof of ownership or a lease (a sales contract or closing document works), and a photo ID. Permits can be applied for before the inspection but are released only after the house passes, and they cannot be transferred. The city counts moving furniture in as occupancy, so a buyer should not start moving boxes early. For general questions, call (314) 291-6550.

The checklist follows the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code plus ordinances adopted by Maryland Heights and St. Louis County. Read it before you schedule and fix the easy items first.

sections.h2: How should I time the inspection, the permit and the closing?
sections.html:
Treat the inspection as the first date on the calendar and work forward from it. A passed inspection starts a 90-day window for the new occupant's permit, so a closing that slips past that window can mean a second inspection.

  • Week one: submit the inspection application and photo ID, then pick up the appointment time the city gives you.
  • Inspection day: arrange for the owner, agent or another named representative to be on site, since lockbox entry is refused.
  • If a Field Correction Notice is issued: fix the items and request the re-inspection. Two re-inspections are covered by the $75 fee.
  • Before closing: the buyer submits the permit application with the sales contract or other closing document as proof of ownership.

The Building Division at (314) 291-6550 can answer scheduling questions. Both sides benefit when the buyer's agent and the seller's agent agree early on who applies.

sections.h2: Which homes does the city inspect when ownership changes?
sections.html:
The rule covers any residential premises, not just houses. Existing multi-family complexes are inspected at a change of ownership, and each apartment is inspected when a new tenant moves in.

The cost for existing apartments is $60 per unit, including two re-inspections. Commercial tenants pay $5 per 1,000 square feet with a $100 minimum. Special cases may qualify for a temporary occupancy permit at the building commissioner's discretion, and Jason Boren's office at (314) 738-2241 takes those requests. A seller who owns a small investment building should check which category applies before setting a closing date.

sections.h2: What does Maryland Heights look like to a buyer?
sections.html:
Maryland Heights is a second-ring suburb west-northwest of St. Louis in St. Louis County. It was incorporated in 1985, and the city is a third-class statutory city run by a mayor and an eight-member council elected from four wards.

The city covers 23.35 square miles, including 1.52 square miles of water. It regulates development in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area, requires a floodplain development permit for any work there, and participates in the National Flood Insurance Program. Its floodplain administrator can say on request whether a property is inside the hazard area and can share the flood zone and base flood elevation shown on the map. Ask for that before you list, because flood insurance is one of the first questions a buyer raises.

Employment is a strong draw. The city's 2022 financial report named Spectrum Mid West, World Wide Technology, Edward Jones, Magellan Health Services and Hollywood Casino St. Louis as its top employers. The Parkway and Pattonville school districts serve the city, and both received Distinction in Performance recognition from the Missouri Department of Education. The population jumped from 5,676 in 1980 to 25,407 in 1990 after incorporation, and reached 28,284 by the 2020 census.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers show about Maryland Heights housing?
sections.html:
Maryland Heights shows 27,559 residents in the Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate, a drop of 2.6 percent from the April 2020 base. Lee's Summit, Liberty and Nixa all grew over the same stretch.

With just 56.8 percent of housing lived in by owners, a large share of local homes and condos are rentals. An investor is a realistic buyer for many properties here, and a condo seller is likely to meet more landlords than first-time buyers. About 81.2 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier, a lower figure than in Nixa or Lee's Summit.

sections.h2: Can I rent out or run a short-term rental from a Maryland Heights house?
sections.html:
A renter needs the same occupancy permit as a buyer, since the city requires one at any change of tenancy. Short-term rentals such as Airbnb have a separate city page and a Short-Term Rental Application.

For a seller who is keeping the house as a rental, this has a practical effect: every time a tenant moves out, an inspection is due before the next one moves in. Selling to a buyer who intends to own the house removes the repeated inspection cycle for you.

sections.h2: How are the deed and property tax handled in St. Louis County?
sections.html:
Deeds are recorded with the St. Louis County Recorder of Deeds in Clayton, and property tax is billed by the county's Collector of Revenue with payment due by December 31.

The recording fee is $26 for the first page and $3 for each added page, with a $25 extra charge when a document does not meet Missouri formatting standards. A mailed deed goes to the Recorder of Deeds at 41 S Central Ave, Clayton, MO 63105, with a check made payable to ROD. If you use eRecording, the vendor may add its own fees.

Property tax must be paid or postmarked by December 31 of the billing year. After that date, interest of up to 18 percent a year and a 2 percent penalty can apply under Missouri law. The Collector's customer portal offers payment plans on delinquent bills. If you sell before the bill arrives, ask your title company how the year's tax will be divided.

faqs.q: Do I need an occupancy permit to sell my Maryland Heights house?
faqs.a: Yes, an inspection and occupancy permit are required at any change of ownership. The seller, an agent, a property manager or a power of attorney can apply for the inspection, which costs $75 and includes up to two re-inspections.

faqs.q: How long is the Maryland Heights inspection good for?
faqs.a: Once the house passes, the new occupant has 90 days to obtain the occupancy permit. After that, a new inspection may be required, so line up the closing date with the permit window.

faqs.q: Can I use a lockbox for the occupancy inspection?
faqs.a: No. City policy does not allow lockbox entry. Someone must be present, and if that person is not the owner or applicant, the application must list them as an authorized representative.

faqs.q: How do I find out if my Maryland Heights house is in a flood zone?
faqs.a: The city regulates development in the FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area and participates in the National Flood Insurance Program. Its floodplain administrator can tell you whether a specific property is in or out of the zone.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in St. Louis County?
faqs.a: $26 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, plus $25 if the document does not meet Missouri formatting standards. A title company usually records it for you.
